'''Kenneth Ownsworth May'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=May |first=Kenneth O. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3138/j.ctv5j02wg |title=Bibliography and Research Manual of the History of Mathematics |date=1973 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |isbn=978-1-4875-8718-5 |doi=10.3138/j.ctv5j02wg}}</ref> (July 8, 1915 – December 1, 1977)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=Charles V |last2=Enros |first2=Philip C |last3=Tropp |first3=Henry S |date=1984 |title=Kenneth O. May, 1915–1977 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0315086084900223 |journal=Historia Mathematica |language=en |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=359–379 |doi=10.1016/0315-0860(84)90022-3|url-access=subscription }}</ref> was an American [[mathematician]] and [[historian of mathematics]], who developed [[May's theorem]].

May was a prime mover behind the [[International Commission on the History of Mathematics]], and was the first editor of its journal ''[[Historia Mathematica]]''. Every four years the ICHM awards the [[Kenneth O. May Prize]] for outstanding contributions to the history of mathematics.

==Early life and education==
Kenneth was born in 1915, the son of Samuel Chester "Sam" May (1887–1955) and Eleanor Ownsworth Perkin. His father, an alumnus of the [[University of Oregon]] and [[Yale Law School]], practised law in [[Portland, Oregon]] beginning in 1913. After earning a [[Master of Arts]] degree from Columbia University, Sam in 1920 began teaching [[political science]] at [[Dartmouth College]], and later at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=JET>C. V. Jones, Philip C. Enros, Henry S. Tropp (1984) "Kenneth O. May, 1915 — 1977, his early life to 1946", [[Historia Mathematica]] 11(4): 359–79
</ref>

At the University of California, Kenneth May was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]] as a junior, and studied under [[Griffith C. Evans]]. May joined the [[Communist Party USA]] (CPUSA) and the [[Institute of Pacific Relations]], of which he served as secretary from 1933. May's mother died in a gas heater explosion at home in 1935. The following year he was granted the [[Bachelor's degree|A.B. degree]] and named to the [[Order of the Golden Bear]]. In 1937 May was granted a master's degree and was selected by the [[Institute of Current World Affairs]] for foreign study. He participated in a Russian seminar and expected to study in [[Russia]], but those plans fell through and he took up study at the [[London School of Economics]].<ref name=JET/>

May was married on July 25, 1938. His wife, Ruth, had a leave of absence from her school for study at the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]], so the couple studied there for a year. In 1939 they travelled, including to Moscow where May visited the Kharkov Engineering-Economics Institute.

== Career ==
Returning to California, May became a teaching assistant, assigned to [[mathematics of finance]] and calculus with [[analytic geometry]].<ref name="JET" /> May's work with the CPUSA led to alienation from his father and dismissal from his job. The affair received attention nationwide and was featured in a [[The New York Times|New York Times]] article.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Professor May Disowns Communist Son; 'Only Honorable Course,' Says Californian| work=The New York Times |url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1940/09/27/94001464.html?zoom=16|access-date=2021-11-26|language=en}}</ref> In 1942 he ran for [[California State Treasurer]] under the Communist banner. May's associations with [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] were used as evidence in [[Oppenheimer security clearance hearing|Oppenheimer's security clearance hearing]]. In World War II May attempted to join up, but until Ruth filed for divorce in June 1942, he could not be drafted. May's unit was sent to [[Kiska]] Island in the Aleutian chain. In May 1944, May married Jacqueline Bromley. His career in the military was recounted on page 4 of ''[[Stars and Stripes (newspaper)|Stars and Stripes]]'' (Mediterranean Rome) on March 3, 1945.<ref name="JET" />

In 1946 May submitted his thesis, ''Mathematical Theory of Employment'' for the Ph.D. He then received a teaching appointment at [[Carleton College]] in Northfield, Minnesota. As a protest against the [[Vietnam War]], in 1966 May signed a vow of tax resistance.<ref>[http://triptych.brynmawr.edu/cdm4/item_viewer.php?CISOROOT=%2FSC_Ephemera&CISOPTR=1585 The Time Has Come (to withhold taxes)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330181249/http://triptych.brynmawr.edu/cdm4/item_viewer.php?CISOROOT=%2FSC_Ephemera&CISOPTR=1585 |date=2012-03-30 }} from Tri-College Consortium</ref> He moved to [[Canada]] the same year.

May is remembered for his ''Bibliography and Research Manual of the History of Mathematics'' (1973) published by [[University of Toronto Press]]. He made editorial contributions to the [[Encyclopedic Dictionary of Mathematics]]. He managed the compilation of an index for the first 80 volumes of [[American Mathematical Monthly]] and wrote numerous book reviews. Philip Enros compiled a bibliography of May's writings that was published in 1984.<ref>Philip C. Enros (1984) "Kenneth O. May — Bibliography", ''Historia Mathematica'' 11: 380 to 893</ref>
